title: The Life and Works of J.D. Salinger
summary: Josh and Chuck profile J.D. Salinger's life and work, from his birth in Manhattan in 1919 and his youth at Valley Forge Military Academy, through his failed college attempts, his tutelage under Whit Burnett at Columbia, and his World War II service (D-Day at Utah Beach, Battle of the Bulge, Dachau, counterintelligence and denazification work). They cover his PTSD, his first marriage to Sylvia, and his Zen and Vedanta spiritual searches. The episode covers The Catcher in the Rye's publication and sales, the Nine Stories collection, and the move to Cornish, New Hampshire, where the 1953 Shirley Hayes-style newspaper interview (named Shirley Blainey in the transcript) triggered his withdrawal into reclusiveness. It also covers his relationships with younger women (Claire Douglas, Jane Miller, Joyce Maynard, Colleen O'Neill), the memoirs by his daughter Margaret ("Peggy") and his son Matt Salinger's rebuttal, and the unpublished work still held back. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Red Stripe beer and a sign-off, with tour announcements at the start.
topics: Catcher in the Rye cover and title meaning

segments.title: Tour announcements
segments.summary: Hosts announce Pacific Northwest live shows in January in Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco, and direct listeners to the website for official ticket links.

segments.title: Opening banter on Salinger
segments.summary: Hosts open with a Greta Garbo quote and discuss reading Salinger, comparing Catcher in the Rye rereadings and Adam Sandler. They note Salinger's approachable style and the mystique added by his disappearance.

segments.title: Catcher in the Rye and Salinger's birth and family
segments.summary: Catcher in the Rye's 1951 release and the word phony are introduced. Salinger is born in Manhattan in 1919 to a distant father and a doting Irish Catholic mother, Miriam. His mother sends an acceptance note for a story when he is eighteen.

segments.title: Schooling and Valley Forge
segments.summary: Salinger attends McBurney Preparatory School, then goes to Valley Forge Military Academy after poor grades. He joins drama, edits the yearbook, and thrives in the structured environment.

segments.title: NYU failure and Europe
segments.summary: Salinger flunks out of NYU. His father sends him to Poland to learn the meat and cheese business, and he instead goes to Vienna, learns German, and falls in love with a Jewish family's daughter. That family does not survive the war.

segments.title: Whit Burnett and writing epiphany
segments.summary: Salinger attends Ursinus briefly, then takes writing classes at Columbia under Whit Burnett, editor of Story magazine, who with his wife Hallie discovered writers like Tennessee Williams, Truman Capote, and Norman Mailer. Hearing Burnett read Faulkner's Sun straight leads Salinger to adopt a plain, understated style.

segments.title: First publications and the New Yorker
segments.summary: Salinger re-enrolls, gets his first story The Young Folks published in Story in 1940, and keeps writing. He wants to be published in the New Yorker, which rejects him seven times before accepting Slight Rebellion off Madison, which is shelved for five years after Pearl Harbor.

segments.title: World War II service and D-Day
segments.summary: Salinger enlists after America enters World War II and is rejected for officer school. He lands at Utah Beach on D-Day with drafts of Catcher in his knapsack, and his regiment suffers heavy losses. He writes about D-Day in The Magic Foxhole.

segments.title: Battle of the Bulge, Dachau, and counterintelligence
segments.summary: Salinger fights in the Battle of the Bulge and is at the liberation of Dachau. He serves as a counterintelligence officer interrogating Nazis, using the German he learned in Vienna.

segments.title: PTSD, Sylvia, and Zen Buddhism
segments.summary: Salinger struggles with battle fatigue and PTSD, checks into a hospital in Nuremberg, and marries Sylvia, a former Nazi party official, though the marriage is short. Back in New York he drinks and dates, then turns to Zen Buddhism. Spoiler warning is given for the ending of Catcher. The hosts note his stories' optimistic endings, such as For Esme with Love and Squalor.
topics: For Esme with Love and Squalor

segments.title: Westport and writing Catcher
segments.summary: Salinger leaves New York in 1949 for Westport, Connecticut, and finishes The Catcher in the Rye. A biographer says he spent ten years writing it and regretted it for the rest of his life. The novel is seen as a war story disguised as a coming-of-age tale.
topics: writing The Catcher in the Rye

segments.title: Catcher sales and publishing experience
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Catcher's sales of about 65 million copies and its royalties. They compare it to the best-selling novels list, with Don Quixote on top. Salinger hated the publishing process and the original cover, and first editions are valuable.

segments.title: Nine Stories and the Ween joke
segments.summary: Nine Stories follows Catcher as a bestseller. The hosts digress into a tangent about Ween's Twelve Golden Country Greats.

segments.title: Meaning of the Catcher in the Rye title
segments.summary: Chuck explains that the title comes from a Robert Burns poem and that Holden sees himself as a catcher stopping children from falling off a cliff into adulthood.

segments.title: Fame and the break
segments.summary: Hosts describe fame bringing reporters, fan mail, and young writers seeking guidance, and say a break is coming.

segments.title: Move to Cornish and the Shirley Blainey interview
segments.summary: Salinger buys property in Cornish, New Hampshire in 1953 and lives a quiet life with local teenage friends. A teenager's school-newspaper interview is published in a regional paper, which makes him build a fence and withdraw, starting his recluse period.

segments.title: Claire Douglas, religion, and his children's accounts
segments.summary: Salinger marries Claire Douglas in 1955 after a relationship that began when she was sixteen. They bond over Vedanta and Hinduism. Daughter Margaret describes him as a strange man, while son Matt says those accounts are gothic tales.

segments.title: Allegations about relationships with young women
segments.summary: Margaret's book Dream Catcher, published in 2000, describes her mother's treatment. Claire divorced him in 1967. The hosts discuss Jane Miller, who was fourteen when the relationship began, and his later relationship with Joyce Maynard. He married Colleen O'Neill in 1992 when she was 21 and he was 69.

segments.title: Joyce Maynard, Peter Norton letters, and unpublished work
segments.summary: Joyce Maynard's relationship with Salinger is described, and she auctioned his letters, which Peter Norton bought for $200,000. Salinger kept writing without publishing. Matt Salinger plans to publish some unpublished work carefully, with more Glass Family stories expected.

segments.title: Further reading and analysis
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a Michiko Kakutani analysis of Salinger's writing that he will send to Josh.

segments.title: Listener mail: Red Stripe beer
segments.summary: Steve writes that a Red Stripe mention in a scuba episode reminded him of a country club event where Red Stripe sold out after a movie scene showed two characters drinking it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck thanks Steve and invites listener emails at the show's address. Credits follow.
